USER TURN 9
hwoever kyoku nee dto diesn hwo ifnromation passes form the toolvm to otehr environemtns

ASSISTANT TURN 9 (1 messages, last privileged)
[earlier] Yes. That communication path is the main design work—not merely installing the SDK. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Tool VM Agent’s Python / TypeScript / shell │ ▼ Portal SDK / CLI — automatically configured │ │ Request + authenticated caller identity ▼ Tool Portal Authorize call; handle required approval; route it │ ┌─────────┼──────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ MCP Credentialed VM Host │ Results / errors / artifact references │ ▼ Tool Portal ──► SDK ──► calling code in Tool VM ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── That is the intended flow, not yet a verified transport design. Tool VM should call Portal, not connect directly to those other execution environments. The design needs to establish: ▸ How the SDK discovers and reaches Portal from Tool VM. ▸ How Portal authenticates the agent without trusting a caller-supplied agent ID. ▸ How arguments, results, and large artifacts cross the boundary. ▸ How approvals, cancellation, timeouts, and connection failures reach the calling code. ▸ How provider credentials remain with their existing owner rather than entering Tool VM. I’ll inspect the existing connection and SDK transports before choosing the mechanism. Python, TypeScript, and CLI should share this same communication contract.

[earlier] The SDKs and CLI exist, but the managed SDK currently connects to a private socket inside Gateway VM—not Tool VM. That socket also carries trusted framework operations, so exposing it wholesale would give the guest the wrong interface. I’m narrowing the design to a Portal-only connection that preserves caller identity, approvals, and result handling.
[earlier] The Hermes research found an existing return path: execute_code sends nested tool requests back through files polled by Hermes. But it is limited to seven hard-coded tools and does not pass the session identity Portal approvals need. I’m comparing reuse of that path with a runtime-owned Portal connection; the choice must keep the SDK reusable, not make it depend on Hermes internals.
[earlier] The transport comparison is now concrete. Reverse SSH port forwarding is disabled by the pinned VM provider, so I won’t base the design on it. The viable reuse path is a bounded request/reply channel over ordinary SSH process streams, with SDK calls bound to the originating invocation. I’m checking the last difficult part: preserving the real conversation for approvals when several conversations share one Tool VM.
[earlier] The design now uses a reusable SDK bridge alongside the trusted adapter. Hermes’s supported middleware supplies the exact conversation; the bridge reuses existing Portal calls and approval handling. The three documents are written with call-flow and boundary diagrams. I’m checking their consistency and transport limits before the independent review.
